hero.filename: Hell's Mouth and the site of RAF Hell's Mouth - geograph.org.uk - 621842.jpg
hero.caption: Hell's Mouth and the site of RAF Hell's Mouth The lighter green fields behind the sandy beach of Hell's Mouth Bay formed RAF Hell's Mouth between 1937 and 1945. A tiny airfield with grass runways, still it accommodated Blenheims and Whitleys and on one memorable occasion a Vickers Wellington X3541 piloted by a Pole. It had combined functions as a training base for bomber crews and airgunners and operated in conjunction with RAF Penrhos. The targets for the bombers were rafts which were floated in the bay, and the airgunners were trained on the ground on a railway borne moving target and in the air on targets towed by aircraft.

images.caption: Windsock 2007 This windsock is on the edge of the southern bank of the former RAF Penrhos. This station was opened in 1937 as part of a bombing school operated in conjunction with RAF Hells Mouth. It proved a poor site, the grass runways were far too short and ended here on the southern perimeter with a twenty foot drop. Planes regularly overshot the runways and ended down this bank. The base which closed in 1945 was bombed 6 times by the Luftwaffe. Since WWII the station has been the home of a Polish community of ex-servicemen and their families. It is also the site of the Wakestock Festival.

images.filename: Approaching Towyn Farm on the Air Ministry built road - geograph.org.uk - 642672.jpg
images.caption: Approaching Towyn Farm on the Air Ministry built road Before the construction of RAF Hell's Mouth in 1936 the road towards Towyn Farm followed a straight line across the fields. It was then replaced by a wide, sweeping road which followed the eastern and north-eastern perimeter of the base. This contrasts with the narrow, twisting lanes towards Llanengan and from Towyn Farm towards Llangian.

images.filename: Sharp bend where the road was diverted around RAF Hell's Mouth - geograph.org.uk - 646500.jpg
images.caption:
Sharp bend where the road was diverted around RAF Hell's Mouth The track in the field follows the line of the old road. With the construction of the airfield in the 1930s, this was replaced by a new and wider road which followed the perimeter of the base. This resulted in a sharp bend into the new section of road which has been the scene of frequent minor accidents.
    Little remains of RAF Hell's Mouth. One of the best surviving features is a fine pill box which can be seen on the airfield's skyline, immediately to the right of the quad-bike.

images.filename: The north-east corner of the former RAF Hell's Mouth - geograph.org.uk - 646923.jpg
images.caption:
The north-east corner of the former RAF Hell's Mouth This corner, now part of Towyn Farm, and used mainly for sheep grazing, is worth recording for two reasons. 
[1].It was at this point against a sunken wall the Polish-piloted Vickers Wellington X3541 of 18th OTU (an all Polish Operational Training Unit), then based at RAF Finningley,(now Robin Hood Airport), nr. Doncaster SK6598), with its crew of six, came to a sudden halt after its belly-flop across the airfield on the 3rd of August, 1944, and 

[2]. It was here also that the farm house of Punt-y-Gwair and its outbuildings stood. The whole were demolished to allow an extension of the airfield at the beginning of WWII.

images.filename: The site of RAF Hell's Mouth - geograph.org.uk - 646589.jpg
images.caption:
The site of RAF Hell's Mouth This view in a southerly direction encompasses much of this former grass airfield which was used as a gunnery and bombing range between 1936 and 1945.
Now peaceful, it was then at times a very noisy, and dangerous, place. Injuries and, at least one fatality, resulted from pilot error. In one night time bombing incident in which a searchlight on the nearby cliffs was being used to illuminate the target - a raft a mile out at sea - the bombs were dropped over the searchlight end of the beam.
